claims.text: Mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its subsets are caused by variations in short-range order.
Mechanical-property differences among the alloys are caused by variations in dislocation interactions.
The specific combination and concentration of constituent elements influence short-range order and dislocation interactions.
The equiatomic quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing.
Removing one or more elements from the quinary composition provides a systematic compositional intervention producing equiatomic subsets.
Short-range order and dislocation density are structural mediators of the composition-dependent mechanical behavior.
Variations in short-range order affect dislocation mobility.
Variations in short-range order affect dislocation interactions.
Changes in dislocation mobility and interactions produce differences in work hardening.
Changes in dislocation mobility and interactions produce differences in failure mechanisms.
The quinary alloy will have higher strength than every tested quaternary and ternary subset.
The quinary alloy will have higher ductility than every tested quaternary and ternary subset.
The predicted superior strength and ductility of the quinary alloy result from a more complex dislocation network.
The predicted superior strength and ductility of the quinary alloy result from increased short-range order.
The hypothesis is intended to apply at room temperature under uniaxial tensile loading.
The hypothesis is restricted to single-phase FCC microstructures without precipitates or other second-phase particles.
